info.title: WebIDE Acorn native builder and project store
info.summary: The one accepted description of this API. Both sides are checked against it.
info.description:
This document is the contract, not a description written after the fact. The TypeScript clients are generated from it and the server is tested against it, so a change to either that this document does not describe fails the release gate.

What is declared here is what a client may rely on. The server may answer with more than this — it does — and those extra fields are not part of the contract and may change. What is declared must be present, and a client reading a field this document does not declare is a defect, because nothing then stops the server from removing it.

There is one identity and nothing proves it. Every route answers for the owner `local`. This is storage and compute on a machine somebody already controls, not an account, and no route should be exposed to a network on the assumption that it is one.

503.description: A refusal, in the one shape every route uses.

code.description: A stable identifier for the refusal. Clients branch on this, never on the message.

correlationId.description: Ties this refusal to the server's log line for it.

message.description: What went wrong and what would fix it, in words meant for a person.

retryable.description: Whether sending the same request again could succeed. False means it never will.

fields.description: Per-field detail where the refusal was about the request body.

Problem.description: The one shape every refusal takes, on every route. A client cannot parse two error formats and should not have to discover which it got.

detail.description: What was found, so a failure names its own remedy.

Readiness.description: One thing that had to be true for a toolchain to be usable, and whether it was.

sandbox.description: What the build is confined to. Declared so a caller can see it rather than trust it.

ready.description: Whether a build sent now could run. False is answered with 503, not 200.

digest.description: Of the manifest itself, so a client can tell one toolchain from another.

ToolchainManifest.description: What a server-side toolchain is and whether it can run. Answered with 503 when it cannot, so a client that ignores the body still learns the truth from the status.

HealthLive.description: The process is running. It says nothing about whether a build would succeed.

unmet.description: Every check that failed, across every toolchain, not the first.

toolchains.description: Every toolchain, in the order they are checked.

HealthReady.description: Whether the service can do its job. 200 when ready, 503 when not.

path.description: Echoed back, so a client can refuse an answer to a question it did not ask.

licence.description: Carried with the text, because a header copied into a project brings its terms with it.

SdkDocument.description: One header or source file from a server-side SDK, read-only.

BuildDiagnostic.description: One thing the toolchain said about the source.

bytesBase64.description: The built bytes, encoded so that a binary survives JSON.

BuildArtifact.description: What the build produced, or absent when it produced nothing. A build that failed answers 200 with a null artifact and its diagnostics, because failing to assemble is an answer and not a transport error.

BuildResult.description: What happened during the build, whether or not it produced anything.

BuildProvenance.description: What went in, what came out and what built it, so a rebuild can be compared rather than trusted.

NativeBuildRequest.description: A build to run. The schema and version are checked before anything else, so a client from another release is refused rather than half-understood.

requestId.description: Echoed, so a client with several builds in flight can tell them apart.

NativeBuildResponse.description: The answer to a build, successful or not.

authenticated.description: Always false in this build. Said in the response rather than left to be inferred, because a client that thought this was an account would be wrong about who can read it.

StoreUsage.description: What the store is, who it thinks you are, and how much of it is used.

parent.description: The revision this was written against. Null for the first.

files.description: How many files the revision holds. The manifest, not the content: a timeline is read far more often than a revision is restored.
Filename to base64 content. Encoded so a binary asset survives the journey.

parent.description: The revision this one was written against. A stale parent is refused rather than resolved, so two workbenches collide instead of one overwriting the other.

confirmProjectId.description: The project being deleted, named again. A deletion that does not say what it means is refused, so a stray request cannot remove somebody's history.

StoreTombstones.description: What has been deleted, and when. Deleting without a trace is indistinguishable from a project that was never there.

StoreCollection.description: What reclaiming space removed. Only content no revision names.

StoreExport.description: Everything one owner holds, history included. Work somebody cannot get out is work the store has taken.

UnmetCheck.description: One check that failed, named with the toolchain it belongs to, so whoever is looking at a not-ready service is told what to fix rather than only that something is wrong somewhere.
